Title: Address by the Governor for Suriname
text: Annual Meeting of the Boards of Governors CALGARY, CANADA Address by the Governor for Suriname at the second plenary session Gillmore Hoefdraad AB-2825 C1I/AB-1276 28 March 2011 Original: English 1. 1 would like to take this opportunity to thank the Canadian Government for hosting this annual event. We have heard a lot of apologies for the weather from our Canadian friends; but, I do not think that anyone felt cold as we were wrapped up in the warm hospitality of our host. 2. 1 also use this opportunity to extend condolences to the government and the people of Japan who have been struck by tragedy just recently. Surinamed5s solidarity and support keeps going out to our Caribbean friends in Haiti, a member of CARICOM, in their endeavor to rebuild their country. We are pleased to note that the IDB has a prominent role assisting Haiti on the path to recovery. 3. These two member countries have been hit by extreme natural disasters, one year after the other. It shows us that in a small and open economy or one of the most developed economies, human and material losses are heavy when nature hits with force. The experience of Haiti in particular emphasizes to us how vulnerable small economies are to natural disasters. 4. Suriname, a small Dutch speaking nation in South America, but historically linked to the islands in the Caribbean has at the moment one of the smallest portfolios in the IDB. However, the new government which took office in August 2010 has at an early stage expressed interest in increasing engagement with the IDB. 5. The increased engagement in the IDB, which we hope will lead to a significant increase in technical cooperation and loans in the coming years, will set the path for further development. This is of strategic importance for us for a number of reasons: First, besides very comfortable lending terms, the technical assistance in prefeasibility, feasibility, or the design of the projects and a careful approach in preserving the environment make investment much more sustainable. Second, working with the IDB gives us the needed credibility that the development process is carefully thought out. And finally, this engagement will help us set the stage to attract reliable and long-term foreign direct investment. 6. Suriname, with a population of just over half a million people, is blessed with different natural resources and as such has experienced high growth rates over the last years. However, like many other small open economies, Suriname also faces challenges. Increased revenues during boom periods have been squandered by inadequate public financial management and the absence of the right checks and balances in the system. Fiscal imbalances, caused by excessive spending in the last two years, recently forced a devaluation of around 20% of the national currency. Other harsh policy measures had to be taken in order to improve the fiscal accounts. 7. Notwithstanding the economic mismatches, we are still fortunate. For 2011 growth of 5% is projected. Large investments are predominantly expected in the gold, alumina, and oil industry. Towards 2015, as these investments mature, they are expected to push up the countryd5s growth potential, and the future looks even more promising. 8. For too long we have been benefiting from high commodity prices for just a limited group of products and have failed to diversify our economy. Decade after decade we have been riding the roller coaster from boom to bust. This is not an isolated story for Suriname. Overall, at this time, our countries are doing well compared to the past decades; we have high growth rates and for some countries the incredible occurred; while desperately seeking FD1 and other investments in past decades, some countries have to set up restrictions today in order to slow the massive inflow of foreign exchange. 9. There is a risk that these good times might end. We should look and learn from countries in other regions that are still suffering from the worst financial crisis in recent history. We need to be prepared. We have to make sure that all incoming FD1 and foreign borrowing is guided towards those projects which will improve our real economy and create employment. 10. This is the time that we need to improve our national institutions and build capacity to guarantee the proper functioning of our economies, based on sound macroeconomic fundamentals. This is the time to increase the physical and intellectual capacity of our population by heavily investing in health and education. We also need to invest in our infrastructure, to improve transport communication and housing for our people. 11. We should avoid unproductive consumption and careless spending. This is also the time that we keep improving our financial systems, which have weathered the recent storms rather well, but have suffered greatly in the past. This is also the time that we should care about our savings and that it is necessary to work towards setting up transparent stabilization funds or sovereign wealth funds. These will be the financial savings that we can fall back upon when hard times come around. 12. We, the authorities, should make the qualitative changes in our society. There is a great need for good auditing and accounting systems to end corruption; we, the authorities, should be held accountable for our deeds. One major area of improvement should be in procurement of goods and services. We need to install proper and efficient public financial management systems. There is a need for a strong private sector, respecting the rules as set out by government, and being the backbone of our economies. This is also the time that we should dedicate more resources towards social welfare; much has been done to reduce inequalities, but we should work together towards eliminating poverty. -2. 13. The countries can not do it alone and certainly not in an isolated way. The 1DB, with its experience and enormous knowledge data base, is an institution in an excellent position to assist and guide countries in completing these goals. The 1DB is also the institution that can promote the integration and can support cross-fertilization among member nations. In this integration process, we all can learn from each otherd5s experiences, both good and more importantly bad. While countries remain in the driverd5s seat regarding their needs, the 1DB should support us in this work through its representative offices. The 1DB should play a leading role to make sure that the current achievements in the economies of Latin America and the Caribbean should lead to higher levels of growth and prosperity. There should never be a d2lost decaded3 again in our history. That is a moral obligation to the upcoming generations. 14. The days in Calgary have been spent very usefully. Seminars have pointed out the successes we have had as a region and also the challenges we face. Let us continue on this path of discussion and count on the IDB in this endeavor. In closing, I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to commend President Moreno and his staff for the excellent work currently been done and would encourage you to continue on this path. -3.

Title: IMF-CARTAC Course on National Account Statistics
text: Remarks at the Opening Session of the IMF-CARTAC Course on National Account Statistics February 6-17, 2012 Gillmore Hoefdraad President Centrale Bank van Suriname I Type text It is my pleasure as President of the Central Bank of Suriname and a former official of the Statistics Department of the IMF to welcome you to Suriname, to begin this intensive two-week course in national account statistics which is jointly organized with the IMF, CARTAC, and the CARICOM. In the aftermath of the international financial crises of the past two decades, and the current economic crisis in several regions in the world, there has been increasing recognition that the availability of comprehensive and timely economic and financial data is essential for the formulation and implementation of sound macroeconomic policies and also that the dissemination of the data to the public at large facilitates investment decisions. Data availability with the needed quality can also reduce the frequency and moderate the severity of future episodes of unusual turbulence in financial markets. The pace of change in the needs of users of statistics in recent years, coupled with uncertainties about the direction, manner, and rate at which these needs will evolve, poses special challenges for the development of statistical systems, especially in situations in which tight resource constraints prevail. It has been a priority of the Central Bank to contribute to strengthen the quality and transparency of Surinamed5s official statistics. Consistent with their mandate, which among others includes guaranteeing price stability and sustainable growth, central banks need to have access to information that is as comprehensive, timely, and accurate as possible in order to carry out their responsibilities. Jointly, the Central Bank, the Ministry of Finance, and the General Bureau of Statistics have also made great efforts to disseminate data of higher quality to the public, together with detailed information on the characteristics of the data. The Evolution of National Accounts. As Frits Bos mentioned in d2 The National Accounts as a Tool for Analysis and Policy, Past, Present and Future"'. d2In the second half of the seventeenth century the first estimates of national income were made. These estimates served clear purposes, like demonstrating that a revision of the English tax system could raise sufficient resources for waging a war with Holland or France.d3 Times obviously are different today: National accounts have evolved over the years. The innovations like the development of the sector accounts, input-output tables and the arrival of the first guidelines were stimulated by the Keynesian revolution and the development of macro-econometric model.building and brought the need of institutionalization and standardization. Just in the nineties, we had the 1993 SNA. Now we are ready for 2008 SNA. The Importance on National Accounts National accountsd1which I consider without doubt the most complicated macroeconomic statistics, because they highly depend on providing information from a wide variety of data sourcesd1are fundamental to tracking and understanding developments that play a major role in economic stability, sustainable economic growth and poverty reduction. As national account compilers, you have the important task of producing statistics that inform policy judgments by the public and private sectors, within and beyond your national economies. You face many challenges: serious economic crises in important regions of the world, the increasing complexity of measuring domestic and cross-border activities; the growing demand for statistics on new activities; the need to balance your data collection strategies and outputs against limited resources; heightened demand for timely statistics; and the importance of maintaining the relevance of your statistical outputs. As we all know, the financial and economic crises experienced since the nineties have underscored the need for timely and transparent reporting of national accounts components and other macroeconomic aggregates. We have a group of around 50 participants which includes statistical sffices, planning bureaus and central banks. We hope that this diversity will add to the richness of the experience. We hope that you will find the course rewarding. As compilers, your experience with the practical challenges of implementing sound statistical methodologies and of relating the national accounts to the BOP, fiscal and monetary accounts will, we believe, encourage a stimulating environment that will challenge both participants and lecturers. Experience has shown that the quality of this exchange between instructors and participants, supported by the accumulated knowledge of both parties, makes for an excellent learning environment. Although you will find the pace of the course intense, please also take some time to enjoy the beauty of Paramaribo and its surroundings. Our officials will be pleased to provide you with all the needed information. May I wish you a satisfying two weeks as the instructors aim to help you improve your skills in all relevant aspects of national account statistics. You will be pressed to read volumes and work very hard. Please accept this opportunity to learn from one another and from your instructors. Thank you!

Title: Opening remarks
text: Opening Remarks by Mr. Gillmore Hoefdraad, Governor of the Central Bank of Suriname, At the IDB Pre-Annual Meeting Bergendal, Suriname, February 13, 2012 I would like to extend a warm welcome to the IDB Governors for the Caribbean Countries, the President of the Inter-American Development Bank Mr. Luis Alberto Moreno, the Executive Vice President Mrs. Julie Katzman, and other members of the IDBs management team. I also extend a warm welcome to our executive directors who without doubt do the work for us in the heart of the organization. It is a pleasure for us in Suriname to host this pre-annual IDB event in such a beautiful place as Berg and Dal which as you might not know yet has been financed by the IDB. I avail myself of this opportunity to extend the best wishes of our President, Mr. Bouterse, for a successful meeting. He would have been pleased to extend his wishes personally at the opening of this meeting; however, he is traveling to Haiti this morning in his function as chairman of the CARICOM. We are delighted to host this regional occasion mostly for two very important reasons: 1. Suriname, although joining the CARICOM relatively recently, has decided to take serious steps forward towards major economic integration with the other member states. Therefore, this is an excellent forum for us to brainstorm and exchange views about our common future; and 2. Suriname sees the IDB as a strong partner which is assisting us in our efforts in achieving major growth. Our country strategy plan for the period 2011-2015 shows an increased portfolio four times the 2006-2010 plan. We are convinced that the IDB, with all their technical expertise and the resources available, can assist our countries in decisively moving from the status of dependency to strong economic independence. This Pre-Annual Meeting Forum in which we intend to discuss the state of development of the Caribbean countries, and explore ways of how the IDB can assist with the furthering of these development efforts is very important as many of our economies are at a cross road. We all as small and open economies are facing major challenges as a severe world economic crisis is looming. Whatever the outcome of the discussions in Europe we can be assured that Europes major task for the coming years will be improving the fiscal accounts of the governments and actions to solve the problems of the sovereign debt. Just this morning we heard about major disturbances in Greece. There are so many lessons to be learned from Europe. The questions that arise are: What is in for us? What are the challenges that we face? Let me start by trying to place the Caribbean in perspective: In this case, I am addressing you not as a Governor of a Central Bank but as a Governor of a development bank which provides for me the opportunity to go beyond monetary policies. What makes us strong? Democracy, and pluralism! A significant strength of the Caribbean is the existence of vibrant democracies. Pluralism and democracy have flourished in the Caribbean, and racial and gender equality have long underpinned the political process. CARICOM countries have healthy competitive political processes, decades of experience with regular national elections, and entrenched respect for civil and economic liberties. Social indicators: The political stability has also been a contributory factor to another of the region's strengths the relatively well-developed social indicators. Education and health indicators in the Caribbean are strong and poverty remains lower than in many other parts of the world. I think that there is a strong consensus in the region that it is important to safeguard these achievements in the current grueling competitive environment. I think that I can make it clear that in the Caribbean we see human capital, continuous creation of capacity, as the single most critical ingredient in making optimal use of the growth opportunities over the longer run. But we should be aware that both education and health are expensive to maintain and that we have to work for it in order to maintain or further improve these standards. That does not mean all is perfect. We face challenges in resolving inequalities in income, battling rising crimes and in general improving the overall standard of living. CHALLENGES THAT WE FACE Most of our countries are facing serious threats. Tourism: It might be the ecotourism or beaches at the sea! We have the ability to seize on emerging comparative advantagessuch as our tourism sector. As the world economy continues to be faced with difficulties, however, and the liquidity of the worlds middle class is diminishing (hereby seriously affecting the affordability to travel/vacation), there is an urgent need to agree on how the region's comparative advantage could be better used to attract tourists. Agriculture: Our efforts in the Caribbean in the agriculture sector are in need of urgent alignment. The erosion of trading preferences with Europe has brought a sustained decline in traditional agricultural export earnings there is an urgent need to explore new markets, and maybe those markets are much closer than we think. Right here in the Caribbean and Latin America! But therefore, we need to make a decisive move from the rudimentary way of producing agricultural products to a industrial form which would include all components of the production chain. We have to aim towards the value added. Labor market: Another challenge is related to the labor market. We need to make sure that our workers are equipped with the skills necessary to compete in today's fast changing global economy: With the large emigration of skilled labor from the region to industrial countries in past decades, the task of ensuring that the retooling of skills to meet the evolving demands of the region is enormous. We should also be thinking of incorporating the experience we have overseas. Financial market: Since independence, the region has strived to develop advanced financial markets that have strong cross-border linkages, but a question you may wish to ask yourselves is: Are these markets being tapped to serve the region's strengths? Lending to high growth sectors still remains relatively low. Public debt has increased rapidly in some of our countries. Unfortunately, the region is now home to several countries with very high debt-to-GDP ratios. Energy: The IMFs regional Economic Outlook of October 2011 mentioned the negative impact of rising oil prices in the Caribbean countries. We all know that Caribbean countries are very worried (and rightly so) that increasing global oil prices will impair their efforts to expand economically. It is, therefore, time to explore new avenues with an emphasis on a more proactive use of renewable energy. In the case of Suriname, I can inform you that this forms part of the Governments priority development agenda, particularly the generation of energy using Surinames hydro potential. THE WAY FORWARD Despite a shared history, and many of the shared experiences since independence that we all know about, there has not been more significant progress at regional economic integration. It is not that the sentiment for integration has been absentindeed, regional integration has been a top agenda item for Caribbean leaders for nearly half a century, but the action has not fully matched the rhetoric. In that regard, I should say that we should finally walk the talk. Our focus on integration cannot be talks anymore but should result in concrete economic action plans which should lead to the integration progress. We must together find ways to define new economic activities, which will allow our countries to finally get on a sustainable development path. We must try to find ways to rationalize our entitlement systems, and look for a more efficient use of our scarce resources. This is the time to combine scarce human, financial, and natural resources to one common goal: bringing prosperity to our nations. There is one final remark that I would also like to make: We should understand that this is not just a government task. We should be looking for ways to engage our private sector in the development process. How do we pave the way for cross-border private sector activities? Spending on education, research and improving technologies should not just be the task of the Government. We need the private sector as a partner, willing to go on the road of development. I will obviously not get too much in detail at this opening speech in regard to my own ideas, but we all should work towards finding solutions to the ever growing list of issues in the Caribbean. It is in this regard that, while we should be responsible for our own actions and being in the driver seats, I am looking forward to the assistance of the Inter-American Development Bank to help us address these issues and to help define common ground to achieve sustainable development. We believe in the IDB, and I think the approval of the Banks capital increase has been, among other issues, our stamp of approval. President Moreno has mentioned several times that this is the decade of the region. We from the Caribbean should seize this moment and without getting lost in the overall statistics, which overshadows many times the small economies, we should make sure that we can also proudly say this is our decade. I wish you a very pleasant stay in Suriname, and hope that you will enjoy our hospitality, our natural beauty, and our cuisine.

Title: Statement Governor at Annual Meeting of Governors at Sudan
text: In the name of ALLAH, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful Distinguished Chairman of the IDB board of Governors Distinguished Governors and Executive Directors of IDB Your Exellency, Dr. Ahmad Mohammed Ali, president of the Islamic Development Bank, Ladies and Gentlemen Assalamu alaikum First of all I would like to thank the Sudanese Government and the people of Sudan for their warm welcome and their hospitality. This should be my fifth visit to Khartoum and it is a great pleasure to be back. Your excellences; It is an honour and privilege for me to address the 37th annual meeting of the Board of Governors of the Islamic Development Bank. Suriname, a small country in the North East of South America, with only half a million in population, but with a historical path that brought an enormous richness in ethnicity and religions, became a member of the Islamic Development Bank in 1997. Although we have a very small portfolio with the Bank, Suriname cherishes the relationship because we see in the IsDB a real partner for development. The world is changing and as the future predicts a predominant role for the emerging economies, Suriname see the partnership with the IDB as part of this future. Suriname, being isolated for decades, is increasing the level of engagement with the rest of the world. As the only member country of the IDB, belonging to the Western Hemisphere, lying in the north east of South America, we see ourselves as a natural bridge between the new world and our fellow members in the other continents. Therefore, I should mention that Suriname would like to support all efforts for more engagement of the IDB and member countries with our region especially now since the President of Suriname, HE Bouterse, is Chairman of the Caribean community, CARICOM, and Suriname is one of the founding members of UNASUR, the south American union of nations. In my brief remarks, I would like to present to you some of our recent economic achievements, share with you our effortsd1 supported by our development partners, including the IDBd1to sustain these achievements by building strong institutions that will last for generations to come. In the past, increased revenues during boom periods in Suriname have been squandered by inadequate public financial management and the absence of the right checks and balances in the system. The current government which came into power in august 2010 faced many challenges. We were forced to devalue the currency by twenty percent in early 2011 and other strong policy measures had to be taken in order to improve the fiscal accounts. One year after these needed measures that were predicated on prudent fiscal policies, we are looking at a stable exchange rate, increase of international reserves with thirty percent, a sharp reduction in the fiscal deficit, and the clearing of all outstanding arrears with bilateral external and domestic creditors. In recognition of these achievements, two leading ratings agencies, Standard and Poor's and Fitch, last year upgraded Suriname, even as other countries in the region and beyond faced serious downgrades of their sovereign debt. The high volatility in our export earnings in the past has been reduced somewhat by the fact that we have succeeded in the last years in diversifying our mining income to 3 separate and largely uncorrelated mining products. It used to be only alumina that we exported, now it is also oil and increasingly important, gold. Currently growth in Suriname is to be sustained at 4-5 percent. Large investments of almost 100 percent of GDP are expected to be made in the near future in the gold, alumina, and oil sectors. Towards 2015, as these investments mature, they are expected to push up the country's growth potential, and the future looks even more promising. We are also strengthening our fiscal framework, with the view to broadening our revenue base and improving public finance management and reporting. Transparency of government operations is a high priority for our government, and we are working with regional and international partners to strengthen statistical data systems in national accounts, public finance, balance of payments, and monetary statistics. Already much data can be accessed online on the Central Bank of Suriname's webpage. It is not only the mining sector. It is also worth mentioning that Suriname is one of the most biodiverse countries of the world, part of the famous Amazone region with vast amounts of sweet water and an enormous potential in the agricultural sector. Learning from our experiences, and observing the current problems the world faces, we are also aware of our low debt-to-GDP ratio and will borrow only where we see clear benefits for growing our economy and investing in our physical and human capital. In Suriname We are working to towards diversifying our economy, increase the standard of living by combatting poverty, keep improving our education and health system, and bringing up our national institutions to optimal standards. We are a small and open economy and are very wary of what the effects of external shocks were and still could be in our economy. Therefore, we should not squander the country's natural resources but use this wealth to build a stronger Suriname and save it for future generations. It is in this vein that the President of the Republic of Suriname, His Excellency President Bouterse, announced in his new years' speech that Suriname established a sovereign wealth fund. Very soon the law which will provide the strict controls of how funds will be saved, invested and used in times of need shall be submitted to parliament. In closing, I would like to avail myself of this opportunity to commend President Ahmad Mohammed Ali and his staff for the excellent work currently being done and would encourage you to continue on this path.

Title: Highlights of 2012 and a Preview of 2013
text: Central Bank of Suriname: Highlights of 2012 and a Preview of 2013 For the first time, the monetary reserves of Suriname have surpassed the magic threshold of one billion U.S. dollars. (Release December 28, 2012) At the end-of-year staff gathering, the President of the Central Bank of Suriname, Gillmore Hoefdraad, indicated that 2012, the 55th anniversary year, has been a remarkable year for the Bank and for Suriname in many ways. In many respects, the year 2012 could be named the Year of Visibility. Suriname has definitely become much more visible to the international and regional community. People looked at Suriname with interested, but critical, glances. Not only did our economic performance attract attention, but the policy pursued was acclaimed. While many countries were still struggling with crisis, the Surinamese economy grew by 4% per cent, the domestic and foreign debt is low, public finances are stable and employment prospects have improved. Our international reserves have increased to over US1 billion and 6 million as at the end of 2012, an increase of nearly US196 million for the full year. For the first time, the monetary reserves of Suriname have surpassed the magic threshold of one billion U.S. dollars. The average monthly inflation amounted to approximately 0.4 per cent, which at the end of December represents an estimated annual inflation rate of 5 per cent. This is ten percentage points lower than in 2011. Again -though the fiscal clock is still ticking towards midnight on New Year's eve -it looks as if the government deficit does not exceed 1 per cent of gross domestic product or might even turn into a very small surplus. Based on the favourable prospects on the macroeconomic front, our international creditworthiness improved. One after another, in 2012, the rating agencies, the International Monetary Fund, the IDB and the World Bank, expressed their great confidence in the ability of Suriname to consolidate its achievements and to stay on course. Perseverance with regard to healthy finances, a sound monetary reserve, small manageable fiscal deficits, are seen as an essential prerequisite for a good investment climate and sustainable economic growth. The Bank also invested in the strengthening of ties with regional institutions. In Paramaribo, two meetings of central bankers in the CARICOM group in Latin America and the Caribbean were held as well as the annual conference for financial and monetary policy and research. Understanding, appreciation and support for Suriname has increased enormously as a result of these events. The Bank's President is said to attach importance to external visibility and solidarity because these are powerful means that enable us to get support and, of course, to give it in times of need. As a small, open economy we become stronger through healthy international integration and learning from others and collaborating with each other. Together with the Ministry of Finance, the Bank took several steps to strengthen the financial system of Suriname. In 2012, important financial laws were adopted for monitoring secure money exchange and external transfers. Modernisation, consumer protection and compliance with external standards will also be continued in future years. The Bank continued its information and training activities. More extensive data and information were made available to the public, such as the Statistical Compendium and the book Ons Geld ('Our Money'). An anti-money laundering training course was held and a start has been made with the establishment of the Financial Campus of Suriname which will support financial specialisation and capacity building. On October 1, the training of 40 young economists in hands-on experience was begun at the Bank, which will soon also be extended to the ministries, departments and other state-owned institutions. Young Surinamese professionals thus are already given an opportunity early in their careers to make a concrete contribution to the economy and society. Looking forward to 2013, the Bank will continue following the world economy with a vigilant eye. The U.S. fiscal cliff, with its far-reaching consequences if no agreement is reached, has the attention, and the concerns of Europe as well. The dollarisation level of Suriname's economy remains a point of concern as it could prove to be a source of contagion. The Bank has therefore decided, as part of its monetary policy, to leave the system of reserve requirements for SRD balances held by banks unchanged, but to increase the cash reserve rate for foreign currency deposits by 5 percentage points in the beginning of 2013. The Bank has also been preparing for modernisation of the monetary policy. In the event of threatened internal or external imbalances, the Central Bank will not hesitate to take any further monetary measures necessary to ensure stability. Undeniably, the course commenced will be continued with respect to innovations in the financial legislation and regulations which should eventually result in sound financial institutions and secure payment, savings and credit transactions. In the offing lies the preparation of several financial legislative products for planning, protection and supervision. These include the draft of the credit bureau law, a revised Foreign Exchange law, a law for supervision of the capital markets, and a law for supervision of the insurance industry. Finally, the Bank has ascertained that it must be an institution par excellence, in order to continuously improve the fulfilment of its enormous tasks. An excellent Parent Bank, supervisor, cashier of the Government, guardian of financial stability and security, a reliable and wise policy partner and challenging employer. The Bank will continue to focus on the structural strengthening of its management and internal organisation. The 2012-2017 strategic policy plan and performance-led control and evaluation are part of this. By means of modern management and further professionalisation, the Bank wishes to make further progress. Tomorrow, the Bank will be publishing the Macroeconomic Developments 2011 and the Abridged Annual Accounts 2011 on its website. This brings the annual reporting by the Parent Bank completely up to date (in 2010, reports had only been published up to 2006). The aim of the Bank in the context of improving the provision of information to the public is to publish semi-annual reports (see 2012) and annual reports in the current year and/or at the latest in the following year. The Central Bank of Suriname looks back on a good year with many highlights and the aim is to continue this positive progress of 2012 in the new year. Notes: 1. Finalized inflation figures for 2012 indicate an end-of-year inflation of 4.1% and an annual average inflation of 5%. 2. The GDP-figure mentioned is an estimate.

Title: Launch of interim member country partnership strategy for Suriname
text: LAUNCH OF INTERIM MEMBER COUNTRY PARTNERSHIP STRATEGY FOR SURINAME, 2014-2015 Vice President of the Islamic Development Bank and Delegation, Minister of Finance, Minister van TCT, Min of Education and People's Development, Directors Guests, ladies and gentlemen, It is for me, Governor for Suriname at the Islamic Development Bank, a treat you on behalf of the government of Suriname to welcome to this special meeting, tookthe official entry into force of the INTERIM MEMBER COUNTRY PARTNERSHIP STRATEGY FOR SURINAME, 2014-2015. A partnership between the Republic of Suriname and the Islamic Development Bank. For this occasion, the Vice President of Operations andsome of his staff members travelled to Suriname specifically. The visit of the Vice President, Mr Sidibe Birama, heralds a new era in terms of its relationship with the Islamic Development Bank. Allow me to first give you some background information about our membership. In 1996 Suriname became a member of the OIC (Organisation of Islamic Countries). Due to the fact that the Islamic Development Bank is one of the specialized institutes of the OIC, Suriname has taken the opportunityto also become a member of the Islamic Development Bank. In 1997, Suriname's membership of the IsDB was a fact. For Suriname it is traditional that the president of the Central Bank, the Governor's position at the Islamic Development Bank. The first project financed by the Islamic Development Bank in 1997 was also a project in the health care, i.e. setting up health centres in the interior. From 1997 to the present, 4 major projects have been financed for a total amount of US 31.7 million. Why is it important to work with institutions such as the Islamic Development Bank (IsDB), Inter American Development Bank (laDB) and World Bank. In addition to concessional financing, these institutes also offer know-how and expertise. (Furthermore, the right check and balances). The IsDB is an established and renowned funding institution that has proven its worth in combating poverty and supporting development in the member countries. In mylast position at the IMF as regional advisor to the Middle East, I have seen up close the many good work of the IsDB in that region. I am therefore strong of it convinced that this renewed cooperation link with the IsDB will benefit the development ofSuriname. Why an Interim Strategy? An Interim Strategy has also been agreed with the World Bank: this is due to the fact that the cooperation with these institutions was on a very low level and the moment that you as a country indicate that youintend to increase the intensity of the cooperation, they first restart it in the form of an Interim Strategy. Within the framework of this Interim Strategy, we are starting with two projects, one in Healthcare and one in Education,where for both projects the funding from the IsDB is projected for US 68 million. Because of the shared responsibility, the Surinamese government will also earn income with at least 10-12% of the projected financing. In addition to financing projects, this cooperation offers several possibilities, such as technical assistance and knowledge transfer. There is also the possibility to let member countries get in touch with each other and to share knowledge of (know-how transfer) with each other. The promotion ofscientific practice is also of paramount importance to the IsDB. I would like to take this opportunity to also reflect on the aspect of project implementation. In my capacity as Governor of the Suriname at the IsDB and the laDB I get to see the reports relating to the slow implementation of projects. Implementation of projects that were calculated for four years, for example, are eventually carried out in eight years and often enough not completely delivered. When I tookoffice in 2010, together with the Minister of Finance, I started the inventory of the Portfolio, the number of projects in progress at the laDB. It turned out that 80% of this portfolio did not function. In cooperation with the laDB, we have worked hard to be among the top three best performing member countries in terms of project implementation. A modest portfolio at the laDB of US 75 million in 2010 was turned into a 5 year strategic plan of US. 300 million andtoday we can proudly say that it is already close to US 500 million. We will therefore keep our finger on the pulse to make a good start and to make these projects a success. Finally, I would like to thank everyone who contributed to the creation of this Interim Strategy. I would like to congratulate the Government of Suriname on the renewed Partnership Thank you very much.

Title: Financial stability Seminar
text: Financial stability Seminar Ladies and gentlemen, It is my pleasure to open the financial stability workshop in Suriname. Following recent global financial crisis, financial stability has become one of the core objectives of many central banks. Indeed, financial stability is now top strategic priority both at the national level (we see countries adopting even special laws on financial stability) and at the international level - where we see an enormous work ongoing on global regulatory reform agenda as committed by G20 and by the Financial Stability Board. In my opening remarks, I want to speak about the interaction of monetary policy and macro-prudential policy. In particular, I want to focus on the role of the Central Bank of Suriname as the responsible entity for both monetary policy and macro prudential policy in Suriname, and on the changing need for instruments reflecting the rapidly changing nature of our economy. i Having the financial stability function under the roof of the central bank is nothing new and has been implemented around the world as a best practice. Our central bank was created to manage both the macroeconomic environment through the use of its monetary policy kit and to supervise the banking system. That is common practice around the world and needs no further discussion, but it is the interaction of these polices and their changing nature of the instruments and the needs for such instruments that has to be continuously discussed. This combination of monetary and supervisory functions reflects the fact that financial stability is an essential and necessary condition for the effective application of monetary policy. A stable and developing financial system with sound and solvent banks is necessary to assure the optimal transmission of monetary policy and thereby contribute to macroeconomic stability. It also allows for an increase in the role that banks play in the Surinamese economy, as stability of the financial system is a precondition for banking sector expansion and financial deepening. This is particularly relevant for Suriname, which has in recent years sharply increased its interconnectedness to the rest of the world. Banks play a crucial role in providing financing to our economy and we want that role to expand. Linking companies and banks to the rest of the world has brought with it significant benefits in market access, human capital, market opportunities, and synergies through the interaction with the 2 global marketplace. But we need to ensure that this increased interconnectedness and dynamism is managed to attenuate the associated risks. There is a clear link between monetary and macro-prudential policies that we need to be aware of to ensure the maximization of those synergies or the minimization of those risks. Both monetary and macro-prudential policies take a systemic perspective aiming at system-wide stability. The interaction between these policies is important, but so are their differences. Objectives and instruments of monetary and macro-prudential policies are clearly different, but there are also important ways in which they carry a mutual influence:  Objectives differ in the way they are quantified and achieved. Price stability can be quite easily quantified, and we have a clear monthly price index that serves as useful guidance, and the central bank has to fulfil this objective symmetrically: not too much inflation, but no deflation either. Financial stability, by contrast, is about avoiding catastrophic events that carry with them high potential costs. Given the binary nature of such events (they either happen or they do not), it is much more difficult to measure them quantitatively in terms of a value or a threshold. We can only measure risks specified by indicators. 3  In terms of instruments, our main tools of monetary policy are reserve requirements and the understanding between the interaction of private plus public sector credit in the economy and the pressures it exerts on foreign exchange availability and the price level. For macro-prudential policy, there are instruments related to the asset side of bank balance sheets, such as loan-to-equity ceilings, non performing loan reserves, and limits on lending to single clients; liquidity-related instruments such as liquidity ratios; and capital-related instruments such as the minimum capital requirements. Yet despite these differences, the two policies undoubtedly have a strong mutual impact. The instruments deployed in one policy domain affect the objectives of the other. For instance, if macro-prudential authorities deploy a stricter loan-to-equity ratio, this would curtail bank lending during a transition period, which in turn would reduce demand for foreign exchange and demand-related inflationary pressures. As an example in the other direction, reducing reserve requirements could encourage excessive risk-taking by banks and have repercussions on financial stability. 4 The two policy domains also interact on a dynamic basis during the process of development of our country. We are experiencing a rapidly increasing interaction between domestic economic entities and the global marketplace and we are seeing a widespread modernization of our economy. At the same time, we want to maximize the benefits that a more dynamic banking system can bring to the economy by facilitating its expansion into previously unbanked areas of the economy. The benefits for the economy of all these changes are substantive, but they bring about new or heightened risks that need to be properly addressed and managed. We are therefore required to adapt our policy instruments to the changing needs of our economy and put in place new and improved policy instruments. On the monetary policy side, we need to add new instruments like Treasury bill auctions and limit the sharply fluctuating credit to the public sector that we experience. Your discussions these days will help us define new instruments on the macro-prudential side or adapt the existing instruments to the changing needs of our economy. Since the beginning of the reform efforts a few years ago, Suriname has become much more connected to the world. Trade and financial links have deepened and most companies and banks have acquired an international perspective. This has brought with it significant gains in efficiency and market access, but it also brought with it the risks of contagion. 5 Suriname's financial sector has weathered pretty well through the global financial crisis primarily due to its low exposure to the international financial markets but also due to a good supervision of its financial sector. However, during the international financial crisis we have seen how contagion risks affected many developing countries and we need to institute macro-prudential norms and instruments to manage these risks and maximize the gains of our newly found interconnectedness to the world. Therefore, despite the great progress over the past several years made by CBvS in embedding modern standards of supervision, the CBvS is more than committed to keep pushing forward the Suriname's financial sector reforms agenda aiming at its suitable convergence with best international regulatory and supervisory principles and practices. We emphasize our current engagement and leadership with regard to ongoing projects such as: Modernizing the payments system of Suriname through introduction of most advanced solutions for real time gross settlement of payments and securities transactions. 6 Modernizing the regulatory infrastructure for the whole financial sector through adoption of regulations and laws according to the best international standards. Accelerating the establishment of the Credit Bureau of Suriname. Accelerating the establishment of the Deposit insurance system. Institutionalization of the Financial Stability Committee and development of the crisis management framework for the Suriname's financial sector. In the context of CBvS's agenda for financial sector reform: I am pleased to inform that the CBvS has established the department for financial stability that is under my direct supervision and as a result a concrete plan has been outlined and approved to promote this strategic function of the CBvS. Certainly, this conference and its content illustrates on our commitment to promote and maintain financial stability in our country. The management and I will be motivating and empowering the financial stability department to come with its first analysis within a short period of time. 7 Having said that, I am confident that I will welcome you in a similar gathering again next year and that in the occasion of publishing first issue of the Financial Stability of Suriname. I am wishing you a productive and successful seminar and for those from abroad also to have a wonderful stay in Suriname. Thank you. 8

Title: Welcome speech of Governor
text: Welcome speech of Governor Gillmore Hoefdraad IsDB day Hotel Torarica Royal Ballroom 13 October 2014 President of the Islamic Development Bank and delegation, President of the Republic of Suriname OFID Representative Chair of the National Assembly Ministers, Members of the Diplomatic Corps, Representatives of the Islamic Associations, Representatives of credit institutions, Representatives from the public and private sectors. It is my pleasure to welcome Your Excellency Dr. Ahmed Mohammed Ali Al Madani, President of the Islamic Development Bank Group, and your delegation to Suriname. I would like to extend a special welcome to all guests for accepting our invitation to participate in this IsDB Day and I would like to express my gratitude to the president of the IsDB for making these events possible. Suriname has been a member of the IsDB group since 1997 and it is worth noting that H.E. Dr. Ahmed Mohammed Ali Al Madani stood at the cradle of this partnership. The first project that was carried out under this partnership supported d2Primary Health Care Centres in the Hinterland" followed by other projects that included "Upgrading the Suriname Air Navigation System at Zanderij", rehabilitating and expanding the port 1 at Nieuw Nickerie and the "Radio Therapeutic Centre of the Academic Hospital". So far, the relationship between the IsDB and Suriname has developed at a modest rate.The IsDB has proven to be a solid financial institute and partner and has been awarded the highest ratings by international credit ratings agencies in recent years. The Government of Suriname has taken notice of these developments and has agreed to involve the IsDB as one of its key development partners in the 2012-2016 National Development Plan. To strengthen the partnership, an "Interim Member Country Partnership Strategy" was put together in November 2013, whereby Suriname and the ISDB would intensify their collaboration based on national priority areas and to promote South-South relations. As a reflection of this new phase in our partnership, we note the construction of the new building of the Academic Hospital of Paramaribo has been launched today, a project that is part of the larger US96.5 million "Health System Strengthening Project." 1. Health System Strengthening Project, for which the Islamic Development Bank will make available an amount of US60 million. For this project, the OPEC Fund for Development will provide US26.5 million, while the Surinamese government will fund the remainder of the US96.5 million project. This project involves amongst others the renovation and equipment of of the Academic Hospital Suriname, the renovation of 5 primary health care centers that will further help decentralize health care, and institutional strengthening and capacity building in the health sector.. 2 A US15.8 million project to reform the technical and vocational education and training is also ready for launch under the auspices of the Ministry of Education. The Government will contribute a further US2.7 million, which takes the project amount to US18.5 million. A newly-established National Training Authority will set up seven practical training centers in various schools, which are being renovated and provided with the necessary equipment. The commission charged with setting up the National Training Authority will also receive institutional strengthening. The Islamic Development Bank is the lead financer of this project. Once these projects have been successfully completed within the context of the "Interim Member Country Partnership Strategy," we expect that a more comprehensive "Member Country Partnership Strategy" will be defined, for which all stakeholders will be consulted. It is worth noting that workshops for the stakeholders will be held on October 14 and 15 to ensure the best possible project implementation and to include all the opinions and views of the stakeholders. In view of how important the success of these projects is to Suriname, I would like to appeal to all stakeholders to participate in these workshops, actively promote your views and interests, and place utmost attention to the information and decisions stemming from these workshops. The success of the projects will be largely influenced by your participation in these workshops. It is in this context of an enhanced partnership that we are holding today this event, the "IsDB Day." Besides the IsDB bank, its 3 associated institutes will be providing details about the opportunities they offer and how they operate. These include the Islamic Research and Training Institute, the Islamic Corporation for Insurance of Investment and Export Credit, the Islamic Corporation for the Development of the Private Sector, and the Islamic Trade Finance Corporation. We will listen with interest to the presentations of these institutes to understand how we can establish fruitful and long-lasting partnerships. Esteemed guests, The IsDB and its associated institutes are here to support the development efforts of the public and private sectors for the benefit of Suriname. It is up to you as individuals or organizations to explore the opportunities that these institutes are able to offer you. I would like to express my hope that today will live up to your expectations and that through your efforts you may become one of the stakeholders that will help define the future "Member Country Partnership Strategy". Thank you. Gillmore Hoefdraad President Paramaribo, 13 October 2014 4

Title: The way forward
text: The way forward Sound Policies and Institutions towards Economic Diversification and Growth Keynote address by Mr. Gillmore Hoefdraad at the 2nd Competitiveness Forum Suriname It is an honor to be present at this 2nd Competitiveness Forum Suriname and to address the forum at such an early stage. Competitiveness was and remains a critical development issue in Suriname, particularly given the unique characteristics of our country. Suriname is highly competitive in certain areas, sometimes at the detriment of the competitiveness of other economic sectors. We are one of the most competitive countries when it comes to the attractiveness of gold mining and offshore drilling. To our knowledge, the new Surgold mine at Merian is the only new large-scale gold mine in active development in the world. This is testament to the unique competitiveness of our country in this sector on a global scale. Similarly, a large number of international oil exploration firms are actively drilling offshore for oil, again a testament of the attractiveness and competitiveness of Suriname as a destination for such types of investments. Nevertheless, being highly competitive in certain areas has proven for many countries an impediment to diversification, as those competitive sectors have a defining influence on labor costs, create appreciation pressures in the economy, and generally lead to the creation of an economic, legal, and regulatory environment that is conducive to that highly competitive industrial sector. In economic theory, the most famous example was the oil and gas industry in the Netherlands that rendered for many years the other sectors of the economy less competitive. For this example, economists call this phenomenon Dutch disease, no pun intended here. In Suriname, we need to counter this high concentration on mining and oil competitiveness by improving the competitiveness of the rest of the economy. This will lead to diversification. We cannot diversify our economy when the non-traditional sectors are not provided with a more competitive environment. And only diversification will eliminate the problems stemming from the commodities sectors, like commodity price shocks in the alumina, gold, or oil sectors, of which Suriname has seen many in the course of its history. Lessening the impact of these shocks will provide an additional stabilization element to the national economy. Stability and a long planning horizon are necessary requirements for investors to move into Suriname. And the more stable our economy appears and the more certainty investors have about the long-term environment in which they will be operating, the more competitive our economy will appear when compared to other economies. That is something we at the Central Bank can work on to support your efforts. Our policies are geared towards maintaining a stable economic environment that allows investors to plan ahead on a long-term basis. Our efforts are geared to maintaining the purchasing power of our currency, maintaining an inflation rate that is comparable to that of our trading partners, and securing and growing a financial system that benefits our economy in the long term through judicious oversight and the modernization of its regulatory framework and technological infrastructure. We are doing our best to render Suriname attractive for national and international investors, but Suriname needs to remove the barriers of entry and the barriers to business-making in Suriname also. The diversification that we are looking for requires at the minimum leveling the playing field for non-mining enterprises. Examples of that are the steadfast reduction of red tape, the streamlining of legal processes, and the minimization of steps that investors face when they want to establish themselves in Suriname. Examples are the elimination of useless barriers to entry and paperwork that is only required because we required it yesterday, forms to be filled that nobody will read, or permits that need to be obtained that could safely be eliminated or combined with other permitting agencies. I am sure investors can provide a long list of examples to the Competitiveness Unit Suriname, which can serve as a blueprint for quick actions. In addition, tomorrow there will be an interesting panel on the importance of a well-functioning legal framework and institutions. Looking at the work that the Competitiveness Unit Suriname has been undertaking since the 1st Competitiveness Forum in February 2013, we cannot but be impressed. The Competitiveness Unit Suriname has spearheaded a number of well-drafted and concise reports on the way forward for Suriname. We are now at the threshold of implementing the recommendations and I expect that the 3rd Competitiveness Forum will report on practical results stemming from these reports. Let us get our respective commitments straight: international competitiveness is marked by a number of factors, most importantly: relative inflation rates and the cost of doing business. We at the Central Bank of Suriname commit ourselves to supporting Suriname's international competitiveness going forward by maintaining low relative inflation rates compared to our trading partners and competitors. That is our commitment and I expect that you will hold us accountable for it at the next competitiveness forum. We in turn expect that all of you will commit to improving Suriname's international competitiveness by measurably reducing the cost of doing business. Let's be more specific: Suriname has not meaningfully improved its standing on the World Bank's "Ease of Doing Business" ranking. In its 2015 report, Suriname is ranked third from the bottom in Latin America and the Caribbean, just ahead of Venezuela and Haiti. We are still ranked 162 out of 189 in the world, the bottom 15% in the world. Even war-torn countries like Yemen, Sudan, and Iraq are ranked higher! Let us be pragmatic here going forward: we need to target the World Bank score and work diligently to improve each of the various items that compose the index, starting with the easiest ones. Low-hanging fruits first. Let's look at them: we are ranked 181 in the world in terms of the ease of starting a business, and are ranked 184 in terms of contract enforceability. We are ranked 178 in terms of property registration and 171 in ease of access to credit. In all of these categories, we are in the bottom 10% in the world. Some of these items might only need to be better explained to investors and our friends at the World Bank. Another one of these categories is access to credit and we are supporting the efforts in this area through the regulatory and infrastructure modernization of the financial system, but also through the establishment of a credit bureau that will provide better information about individual and corporate creditworthiness. Establishing that credit bureau will move Suriname up into the ranks of the 129 countries that have a credit registry. Last and certainly not least, your efforts can also help to directly target some of the other categories in the index, in particular through streamlining of regulations, elimination of useless barriers to entry, and greater transparency and information-sharing. I look forward to the deliberations in this 2nd Competitiveness Forum Suriname today and tomorrow and am quite certain that the results of your efforts will be reported upon at the 3rd Competitiveness Forum Suriname.
